practicalQuestion: During a seven-day travel period with two competitions, limited food access, and athletes with different playing-time demands, how should performance nutrition prioritize and individualize fueling, hydration, recovery, and supplement decisions while protecting sleep and gastrointestinal tolerance?

decisionContext.population: Collegiate roster with high-minute, low-minute, and returning athletes
decisionContext.outcome: Create an operational nutrition plan that supports readiness across subgroups
decisionContext.constraints: Fixed travel and hotel meals; limited refrigeration; variable minutes and sweat response; supplement and clinical decisions require appropriate review

evidenceConfidence.rationale: An elite football consensus statement and a professional rugby league review give consistent, fairly direct guidance on carbohydrate, protein, fluid and gut comfort across congested competition periods. Meta-analyses add useful bounds on caffeine, antioxidants and melatonin. Gaps remain. No source studies collegiate athletes, female athletes or a travel week with two competitions. No source tests nutrition plans individualized by playing minutes. Sources disagree on recovery supplements.

dimensions.sourceReview: One consensus statement (elite football), one narrative review (professional male rugby league), systematic reviews or meta-analyses on hydration and glycogen, caffeine, antioxidants, melatonin and beer, a two-player case study (elite male Australian Football), and cohort studies of professional soccer load and professional rugby union travel.
dimensions.directness: Moderate. Fueling, hydration and pre-competition meal guidance address congested team-sport schedules directly. Subgroup individualization by minutes is inferred from load data, not tested as a nutrition strategy.
dimensions.consistency: Consistent on high carbohydrate availability, rehydration and food first. Inconsistent on recovery supplements such as polyphenols, antioxidants and melatonin. The hydration and glycogen meta-analysis had very high heterogeneity.
dimensions.transferability: Mostly professional male soccer, rugby and Australian Football players. Several meta-analyses pooled recreational participants. Travel evidence comes from long-haul, multi-time-zone trips. Transfer to a collegiate mixed roster on shorter trips is uncertain.

bottomLine.text: For a two-competition travel week, the library supports a food-first plan. Keep carbohydrate and fluid high around competitions and between games, use easily digested pre-competition meals that athletes have practised, and rehydrate after each competition. Playing time drives weekly load, so plans should reflect each athlete's actual load. Antioxidant and melatonin recovery supplements have weak support, and any supplement use needs formal review because whole-team use carries team-level anti-doping risk.

recommendedDirection.text: If competitions fall within about 2 to 4 days of each other and food access is fixed, prioritize a food-first carbohydrate, protein and fluid plan: higher carbohydrate in the 48 to 72 hours between games, practised easily digested pre-competition meals, and carbohydrate plus protein soon after each competition. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): scale portions to each athlete's playing load rather than one roster-wide amount, and handle supplements as a separate, reviewed decision instead of a default.

actions.title: Set carbohydrate and protein by day and load
actions.text: Source starting values: 6 to 8 g/kg BM carbohydrate is listed for congested fixture periods to replenish glycogen over 48 to 72 hours. For 80 to 120 kg professional rugby league players, the review suggests 1 to 4 g/kg carbohydrate plus 0.25 g/kg protein 1 to 4 hours before competition, and about 1.0 to 1.5 g/kg carbohydrate plus 0.25 to 0.55 g/kg protein within 0 to 2 hours after. Ensure competition is undertaken with high carbohydrate availability. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): treat these as ranges and adjust down for low-minute athletes, whose weekly load is lower.

actions.title: Design pre-competition meals for gut comfort
actions.text: Choose easily digested pre-competition meals and avoid rigid strategies aimed only at hitting carbohydrate targets. Practise competition-day fueling in training or lower priority competitions before travel. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): pre-order familiar options from fixed hotel and travel menus and pack shelf-stable carbohydrate.

actions.title: Individualize fluid and sodium
actions.text: Sweat rates vary greatly between players. Rehydrate after each competition: dehydration reduced short-term glycogen restoration in cited studies, and poor rehydration may raise glycogen use in the next session when performance is needed over consecutive days. Without specialist support, use ample fluids and high sodium and potassium foods.

actions.title: Protect food safety with limited refrigeration
actions.text: The UEFA statement links illness risk to hygiene focused on cross-contamination, cleaning, chilling and cooking. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): do not hold perishable recovery foods without chilling; favor items safe at room temperature.

actions.title: Route supplement decisions through review
actions.text: For the reviewing staff: caffeine showed a small pooled benefit at under 3 and 3 to 6 mg/kg but not above 6 mg/kg. Antioxidants were not effective for soreness, and tart cherry was null after two rugby matches. Melatonin did not improve performance. Whole-team supplement use carries team-level anti-doping risk. The evidence does not test caffeine timing against sleep on travel nights.

monitoring.label: Morning hydration check
monitoring.text: Record body weight, thirst and urine colour each morning of the trip.

monitoring.label: Playing load by subgroup
monitoring.text: Track minutes and external load, since athletes with more match time accumulated more weekly load. Use this to adjust portions between high-minute and low-minute athletes.

monitoring.label: Gut tolerance
monitoring.text: Log gastrointestinal complaints after pre-competition meals and after any approved supplement. In one review, tart cherry juice caused mild gastrointestinal distress in one of 26 participants.

monitoring.label: Sleep and readiness after overnight travel
monitoring.text: After overnight long-haul travel in professional rugby players, sleep was cut on the travel night and drop jump stayed lower until the third day away. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): track sleep and readiness after any overnight leg.

guardrails.text: This brief does not approve any supplement or set policy. Supplement and clinical decisions stay with the appropriate sports medicine, dietitian and compliance review, because whole-team supplement use can put the entire team at anti-doping risk.
Do not use alcohol as recovery hydration. Normal alcoholic beer is inadvisable as the sole rehydration source after a fluid deficit of 1.5% body mass or more.

Treat source numbers as starting ranges, not prescriptions. The rugby league targets were for 80 to 120 kg professional players, and the authors note data may not support sport-specific recommendations.

limitations.text: Studied populations are mostly professional male soccer, rugby league, rugby union and Australian Football players. No source studies collegiate or female athletes in a travel week.
Evidence that in-game carbohydrate spares glycogen is a two-player case study, and the player who used water only also played more minutes.
The hydration and glycogen meta-analysis found no significant pooled effect of rehydration versus staying dehydrated, with very high heterogeneity.
Travel evidence comes from long-haul and multi-time-zone trips, which may not match a shorter domestic trip.

whatCouldChange.text: A study testing nutrition plans individualized by playing minutes in collegiate team-sport athletes could confirm or change the subgroup approach.
Trials of recovery supplements in elite athletes could change the current weak support for antioxidants and melatonin.
Evidence on caffeine timing and sleep during travel would clarify how to use caffeine without harming sleep.

evidenceTension.text: The rugby league review lists polyphenols among supplements that potentially improve recovery, yet the same review reports tart cherry had no effect after two matches in 11 professional players, and a Cochrane review found antioxidants were not an effective strategy for soreness, with no elite athlete data. The melatonin authors conclude it improves recovery, but performance outcomes were null and the only increased outcome was one enzyme marker. On hydration, cited studies found dehydration reduced short-term glycogen restoration, while the pooled meta-analysis effect was not significant and highly heterogeneous.

assumptions: Returning athletes is read as athletes returning from injury, illness or a layoff; the context did not specify.
Travel is assumed to be mostly domestic with few time zones crossed; whether any leg is overnight or long-haul was not specified.
The two competitions are assumed to be about 2 to 4 days apart within the seven-day window.
coverageGaps: No studies of collegiate or female athletes managing nutrition across a travel week with two competitions.
No studies testing nutrition plans individualized by playing minutes (high-minute versus low-minute athletes).
No evidence on nutrition for athletes returning from injury, illness or layoff during travel.
No evidence on caffeine timing and sleep during travel, or on travel-specific gut tolerance strategies.
No evidence on practical food access or storage with fixed hotel meals and limited refrigeration.

Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): for athletes returning from injury or illness, nutrition plans, progression and clearance decisions stay with the treating clinicians and the dietitian. This pack has no evidence specific to them.
